title: The Best Accounting Software for Restaurants, Bars and Cafes to Stop Reconciling by Hand
summary: Still reconciling POS deposits by hand? We compared the 7 best accounting software for restaurants in 2027 so your books close on time, not at 2 a.m.
body_markdown:
***Disclosure*** *: Synder makes one of the tools below; every tool is judged on the same criteria.*


Choosing the best accounting software for restaurants starts with three questions you probably already ask. Why doesn’t a Toast or Square deposit match the day’s sales? Which of your locations made money last week? And can you get daily POS sales into your accounting software without retyping a Z-report?


Card processing fees help explain the difference between sales and deposits. According to the[National Restaurant Association](https://restaurant.org/issues-and-advocacy/policy-brief-swipe-fees) , processing credit card transactions is the third-largest operating expense for most restaurants, after food and labor. Those fees are deducted before card deposits reach the bank.


Restaurant accounting software needs to record those fees alongside daily sales, tips and taxes, so the books can explain the deposits and show how each location is performing. We compared seven tools to see how they handle that work.


## **TL;DR**


- Pick the type of software (ledger, all-in-one platform or add-on) before the brand.
- If your accountant already works in a ledger, you may only need an add-on.
- Ask how the software gets POS sales, fees and deposits into your ledger.
- Choose software that posts fees, refunds and tips on separate lines.
- Check that the software tags every entry with its location.
- Test the software on one real day before you commit.


For a quick recommendation, here’s which tool fits each setup.


## **The best restaurant accounting software at a glance**


The right restaurant accounting software depends on whether you need a ledger, a way to post daily POS sales, or help managing supplier bills. These are our picks for each situation:


- **Your accountant already works in QuickBooks:** QuickBooks Online.
- **Your bookkeeper works in Xero:** Xero.
- **You have several legal entities to consolidate:** Sage Intacct.
- **You want one platform that replaces your ledger and handles the whole back office:** Restaurant365.
- **You want to keep QuickBooks or Xero and stop typing in daily POS sales:** Synder.
- **Your kitchen deals with lots of invoices and tracks food cost daily:** MarginEdge.
- **You pay many vendors and bills across locations:** Ottimate.


Compare the tools by type before you compare their prices. A general ledger, an add-on and an all-in-one restaurant platform handle different parts of the work.

## **How to choose restaurant accounting software**


For a restaurant group with four Square locations that already uses QuickBooks Online, switching to a new accounting system may be unnecessary. A more practical option is to automate how daily sales, tips and fees reach QuickBooks, which is why choosing the right type of software matters as much as choosing the product itself.


### **Ledger, all-in-one or add-on: 3 types of restaurant bookkeeping software**


Restaurant accounting software falls into three types, and some can be used together. If you’re looking for the best restaurant bookkeeping software, the first decision is which of these types you need. Bookkeeping software records daily sales, deposits and bills; restaurant financial software adds reporting, payroll and tax. The three general ledgers in this comparison are online systems that let owners and accountants work in the same file.


**Type** **What it does** **Choose it if** **Watch for**


General ledger (QuickBooks Online, Xero, Sage Intacct) Keeps the books: chart of accounts, bills, bank, reports Your accountant or bookkeeper already uses it No recipe costing; POS sales need a connector or manual entries


All-in-one restaurant platform (Restaurant365) Replaces your ledger with a restaurant-specific ERP that adds inventory, recipes and labor You want one system for the whole back office Moving your books off your current ledger


Add-ons: POS-to-accounting connector (Synder) and AP & invoice automation (MarginEdge, Ottimate) Post data into the ledger you keep You keep your ledger and want one manual step automated An add-on still needs a ledger behind it


A POS-to-accounting connector takes sales, tips, taxes, fees and deposits from the point-of-sale system and posts journal entries to the existing ledger.


For restaurants keeping their current ledger, the POS connection deserves particular attention. An incorrect setup can mix fees, tips and refunds into daily sales entries and leave deposits difficult to reconcile.


### **Restaurant accounting system checklist: what to check before you buy**


A demo or free trial is a chance to test a real day of restaurant activity, rather than relying on a feature list. These six checks also form the criteria used in our method section.


1. **Does it connect to your POS?** Check whether Toast, Square for Restaurants or Clover POS connects natively or needs an add-on.
2. **Does one day tie out?** Pick a day and check that the deposit matches the POS report without manual edits.
3. **Where do tips go?** Tips should post to tips payable, the money you owe staff, not to revenue.
4. **Is sales tax tracked by location?** Each location’s tax should post to the right liability account.
5. **Can every entry carry a location?** Look for QuickBooks classes or locations, or Xero tracking categories.
6. **What will it cost you?** Price it at your real monthly transaction count and number of locations.


If you also need recipe-level food costing, add that to the test. General ledgers don’t handle recipe costing, so you’ll need Restaurant365, MarginEdge or a comparable restaurant tool.


## **7 best accounting software for restaurants in 2027**


The seven products are grouped by software type, not ranked against one another. Each review covers the same practical questions: what the product does, why restaurants choose it, where its limits are, and when another option is likely to fit better.


### **1. QuickBooks Online: best for restaurants whose accountant already works in QuickBooks**


***Source:*** *QuickBooks Online – YouTube channel*


[QuickBooks Online](https://quickbooks.intuit.com/) is Intuit’s cloud-based general ledger. For restaurants, the choice of plan depends largely on how many locations need reporting and how many people need access.


**Type:** General ledger · **POS:** via apps and connectors · **Ledger:** itself · **From:** $38/mo · **G2:**[4.0/5 (3,908 reviews)](https://www.g2.com/products/quickbooks-online/reviews)


**Why restaurants choose it:**


- Plus ($140/mo) supports up to 40 classes and locations combined, allowing restaurants to produce a P&L for each location.
- Advanced ($340/mo) removes that tracking limit and supports up to 25 users.
- Bookkeepers can manage a restaurant’s file alongside their other clients in QuickBooks Online Accountant.


**Watch out for:**


- Simple Start (38/month)andEssentials(85/month) don’t track classes or locations at all.
- Recipe costing isn’t included, and getting daily POS sales into the ledger requires a connector or manual journal entries.


**Skip it if:** You want food cost, inventory and accounting in one restaurant platform.


### **2. Xero: best for restaurant groups whose bookkeeper works in Xero**


***Source:*** **Xero Accounting Software – YouTube channel**


[Xero](https://www.xero.com/us/) is a cloud-based general ledger. Its US plans are called Early, Growing and Established.


**Type:** General ledger · **POS:** via apps and connectors · **Ledger:** itself · **From:** $27/mo · **G2:**[4.4/5 (1,854 reviews)](https://www.g2.com/products/xero/reviews)


**Why restaurants choose it:**


- Xero has no per-user license fee, so a manager or bookkeeper can be added without another user charge.
- Tracking categories let restaurants label transactions by location.
- Growing ($59/mo) removes the Early plan’s caps on bills and invoices.


**Watch out for:**


- Early ($27/mo) allows only 5 bills and 20 invoices, which is unlikely to cover a restaurant’s supplier activity.
- Recipe costing isn’t included, and daily POS sales need a connector or manual journal entries.


**Skip it if:** Your accountant only works in QuickBooks, or you need to consolidate several legal entities.

[Synder](https://synder.com/industry/restaurants/) posts Toast, Square and Clover sales into QuickBooks Online, Xero or another existing ledger.

[Restaurant365](https://www.restaurant365.com/) combines restaurant accounting with operational tools. It includes its own general ledger and a chart of accounts designed for restaurants.

**Why restaurants choose it:**

### **7. Ottimate (formerly Plate IQ): best for groups** **with many vendors and bills across locations**


***Source:*** *Ottimate*


[Ottimate](https://ottimate.com/) automates accounts payable, including invoice capture, payments and approval workflows. It works alongside an accounting system rather than functioning as a ledger.


**Type:** AP & invoice automation · **POS:** not the focus · **Ledger:** through accounting integrations · **From:** contact sales · **G2:**[4.6/5 (210 reviews)](https://www.g2.com/products/ottimate/reviews)


**Why restaurants choose it:**


- Invoice line items can be captured and mapped to general ledger accounts.
- Vendors can be paid by check, ACH or virtual card.
- Approval workflows can route invoices according to vendor, department or amount.


**Watch out for:**


- Ottimate doesn’t publish its pricing plans.
- It handles AP, so POS sales still need another route into the ledger.


**Skip it if:** Your restaurant has few enough suppliers to manage bills directly in QuickBooks Online or Xero.

In Synder’s analysis of customer food and beverage businesses, Square (50.0%) and Clover (46.7%) were the most common POS systems, and 86.7% kept their books in QuickBooks Online.

## **Bookkeeping for restaurants: how daily sales reconciliation works**


Daily restaurant reconciliation checks whether POS sales and bank deposits agree after accounting for sales tax, tips, refunds and processing fees.


Processing fees are a significant expense for restaurants. More than nine in ten operators cite food, labor, insurance, energy and swipe fees as significant challenges, according to the[National Restaurant Association’s 2026 State of the Restaurant Industry](https://www.restaurant.org/research-and-media/media/press-releases/persistent-cost-increases-and-enduring-demand-will-shape-the-restaurant-industry-in-2026) release. The association’s chief economist, Dr. Chad Moutray, said:


> Success for operators this year will hinge on their ability to get the math right in a still-challenging economic environment.
>
>
> Dr. Chad Moutray, Chief Economist of the National Restaurant Association


Delivery platforms introduce another deduction. According to an[NRA survey from May 2026](https://restaurant.org/getmedia/f925bcf1-9195-401d-9a1f-341e0e1e5b31/National-Restaurant-Association-Comments-FTC-Online-Food-Delivery-05182026.pdf) , two in three restaurant operators reported paying average third-party delivery commissions of 15% to 29.9% per transaction. Those commissions are deducted before the payout reaches the restaurant.


A daily reconciliation follows four steps:


1. **Pull the day’s POS sales.** Start with the Z-report, the end-of-day POS report showing sales, taxes, tips and payment methods.
2. **Post gross sales to a clearing account.** This temporary balance sheet account holds sales until the matching deposit arrives, then returns to zero.
3. **Split the deposit.** Card payments are processed through end-of-day batch settlement, with processing fees and refunds deducted before payout. Record sales tax payable, tips owed to employees, processing fees and refunds separately.
4. **Match the net deposit to the bank.** Compare the expected amount with the actual bank deposit and record any difference as a deposit adjustment.


QuickBooks users may consider putting POS payments into Undeposited Funds. This account holds payments until a deposit is recorded, but it doesn’t automatically account for processing fees deducted before settlement. Without a separate fee entry, the grouped payments won’t match the bank deposit.


Here’s how one day of sales at a single location might reconcile. The amounts are rounded to make the calculation easier to follow.


**Example: one day, one location** **Amount**


Food sales $3,000


Beverage sales $1,200


Discounts and comps −$200


Net sales $4,000


Sales tax collected (8%) $320


Card tips owed to staff $600


Total collected at the POS $4,920


Cash sales taken in the drawer (counted $395, deposited separately) −$400


Card payments in the clearing account $4,520


Card processing fees −$130


Refund of an earlier check −$50


Expected card deposit $4,340


Bank deposit $4,340 (difference: $0)


The expected deposit matches the bank because the $130 in processing fees and $50 refund have been recorded separately. Leave either amount out and the deposit appears short, with no corresponding entry to explain the difference.


### **What a daily sales entry should look like**


After reconciling the day’s activity, the amounts can be recorded in the ledger as two entries per location: one for the day’s sales and one for the deposit. Here’s how the same example would appear, with each line tagged to the appropriate location.


**Entry 1: the day’s sales**


**Account** **Debit** **Credit** **Location**


POS clearing account (card payments) $4,520 Location A


Cash deposit $395 Location A


Cash over/short $5 Location A


Discounts and comps $200 Location A


Food sales $3,000 Location A


Beverage sales $1,200 Location A


Sales tax payable $320 Location A


Credit card tips payable $600 Location A


Total $5,120 $5,120


The drawer held $395 against $400 in cash sales, so the $5 shortfall posts to cash over/short.


**Entry 2: the card deposit**


**Account** **Debit** **Credit** **Location**


Bank $4,340 Location A


Card processing fees $130 Location A


Refunds $50 Location A


POS clearing account $4,520 Location A


Total $4,520 $4,520


After the deposit entry, the clearing account is back to zero.


There are three additional setup decisions to consider:


- **Daily summary or per transaction:** One entry per day per location keeps the ledger manageable. Per-transaction posting is useful when every individual check needs to appear in the books.
- **Tip records:** Accurate tip tracking also matters for payroll and taxes. Under the “No Tax on Tips” deduction, employees can deduct up to $25,000 in qualified tips, including shared tips, according to the[IRS](https://www.irs.gov/newsroom/what-the-no-tax-on-tips-deduction-means-for-you) (March 5, 2026).
- **A test month for bookkeepers:** Run the previous process alongside the new setup for one month and compare the results day by day.


## **Multi-location groups, bars and cafes**


For restaurants with multiple locations, each accounting entry needs to be assigned to the correct site. The software also needs to support the volume of transactions generated across the group.


### **Running several locations**


Location reporting depends on accurate transaction tagging. Without it, a restaurant group can’t produce reliable P&Ls for individual sites.


In QuickBooks Online, class and location tracking begin with Plus, which supports a combined total of 40 classes and locations. Advanced removes that limit.


The main approaches are:


- **QuickBooks Online:** Assign daily entries to classes or locations and run a P&L by location.
- **Xero:** Assign transactions to locations using tracking categories.
- **Several legal entities:** Maintain a ledger for each entity, record intercompany transactions and prepare consolidated P&Ls using Sage Intacct.


Location tags don’t account for shared expenses automatically. A central kitchen or head office may support multiple sites, so its costs need to be allocated across locations to get an accurate view of profitability.


### **Accounting software for bars, pubs and cafes: what changes**


Bars, pubs and cafés use many of the same accounting entries as restaurants, but they often process large numbers of relatively small transactions. That can make transaction limits particularly important when comparing accounting software for cafes. Synder’s Basic plan, for example, includes 500 synced transactions.


Beverage revenue also needs to be categorized. The Uniform System of Accounts for Restaurants (USAR), published by the National Restaurant Association, provides a standard restaurant chart of accounts with separate categories for different beverages.


**Account** **Type**


Beer sales Revenue


Wine sales Revenue


Liquor sales Revenue


Beverage cost of goods sold: beer, wine, liquor Cost of goods sold


These accounts support pour-cost calculations. Pour cost is the cost of liquor poured divided by the revenue from those drinks, with inventory counts supplying the cost figure.


Bars also need to track pooled tips as a liability until staff receive them through payroll.


If a bar uses a POS such as TouchBistro, sales still need to reach the ledger through the POS system’s export or a third-party connector, just as they would with Toast or Square.


Catering accounting software has a different focus. Caterers invoice clients for events instead of closing a POS day, so a general ledger with invoicing, such as QuickBooks Online or Xero, covers most of the work, and daily POS posting matters less.

## **Bottom line: which restaurant accounting software should you choose?**


The best bookkeeping software for restaurants depends on what your business already uses and which tasks still require manual work.


- **You want to keep QuickBooks or Xero:** Automate daily POS posting with a connector.
- **You have several legal entities:** Consider a multi-entity ledger such as Sage Intacct.
- **You want one platform that includes food cost:** Restaurant365 combines accounting with restaurant operations.
- **Your kitchen is invoice-heavy:** Add MarginEdge or Ottimate to your ledger.


Before committing, run one real business day through the software. Compare the resulting entries with your POS report and check that the expected deposit matches the bank to the penny.


## **FAQ**


### **Is QuickBooks Online enough for a restaurant?**


QuickBooks Online can serve as a restaurant’s general ledger. Multi-location reporting requires Plus (140/month),whichsupportsupto40combinedclassesandlocations,orAdvanced(340/month), which provides unlimited tracking. Daily POS sales still need to reach QuickBooks through a connector or manual journal entries.


### **How much does restaurant accounting software cost?**


Restaurant accounting software uses several pricing models. General ledgers charge monthly subscriptions, with QuickBooks Online starting at $38/month. Per-location tools such as MarginEdge cost $350 per location per month. Restaurant365 and Ottimate use custom quotes. POS connectors may charge based on transaction volume, with Synder starting at $52/month billed annually. Prices were checked on November 10, 2026.


### **How should a restaurant record tips?**


Tips collected for employees should be recorded as a liability in a tips payable account, not as restaurant revenue. The liability is cleared when tips are paid through payroll. The daily sales entry example includes the corresponding tips payable line.


### **How do you record DoorDash and Uber Eats payouts?**


Record gross delivery sales, recognize the platform’s commissions and fees as expenses, and account for the net payout through a clearing account. Synder doesn’t currently offer direct integrations with DoorDash, Uber Eats or Grubhub, so those transactions need to remain in the restaurant’s existing process.


### **What should a bookkeeping firm look for in a POS-to-QuickBooks sync tool?**


A bookkeeping firm should look for five things: no missing business days, mapping to the client’s existing accounts, totals that reconcile to the POS end-of-day report, the ability to run a test month before going live, and a dashboard for managing multiple clients.
